BUDGET REPORT 2026 
TUARASCÁIL BUISÉD 2026 
 
 
 
Is dúshlán mór é Buiséad a ullmhú don bliana seo arís mar thoradh ar deacrachtaí 
shuntasacha atá roimh d'airgeadas na Comhairle i 2026. 
Agus an Buiséad á ullmhú, cuireadh béim ar thacaíocht do na Ceantair Bhardasacha agus 
cothromú a dhéanamh ar na riachtanais mhéadaithe ar na bpríomhsheirbhísí ar fad chun 
leanúint le forbairt na mbailte agus na pobail tuaithe sa Chontae. 
Trí Bhuiséad 2026, tá leithdháileadh de acmhainní dírithe ar na réimsí tosaíochta agus na 
réimsí ina bhfuil siad ag teastáil is mó. Ar an mbealach sin, úsáidfear an t-airgead atá ar 
fáil, déanfar riachtanais a tiomantas a mhaoiniú, agus déanfar cistí roghnacha a dháileadh 
sna háiteanna is gá. 
 
Introduction  
The Draft Budget for the financial year 2026 is presented to the Members of Cork County 
Council in compliance with the statutory framework, Local Government Act 2001 (as 
amended) and relevant regulations. The Draft Annual Budget 2026 Report, and tables 
therein, outline the growing investment the Council will make in the operation and 
delivery of services to our citizens, and the enhanced support to the sustainable 
development of our communities. 
Cork County Council’s Draft Annual Revenue (day to day operational) Budget for the 2026 
financial year amounts to €530m, an increase of €14m over the 2025 Budget of €516m. 
This investment, and increase over 2025,  reflects Cork County Council’s commitment to 
deliver the services needed to enhance our urban and rural communities.

iv 
 
The Draft Budget 2026 is reflected in the statutory tables as detailed herein and 
presented to Members for adoption at the Annual Statutory Budget Meeting of 10th 
November 2025.  
 
In accordance with the Local Government Act 2001 (s135) the proposed Capital 
Programme for the period 2026 – 2028 will issue to Members under separate cover. The 
Capital Programme outlines an ambitious programme of projects with a potential 
investment of over €1.3bn in the County over the next three years.  
 
Strategic Context  
The Draft Budget 2026 has been prepared in consultation with the Members, with the 
intent of meeting the objectives, as adopted by Cork County Council, of the Corporate Plan 
2025–2029,  the County Development Plan (CDP) and the Local Economic and 
Community Plan (LECP), and includes: 
• Providing funds for the continuation and enhancement of service delivery levels, 
including increased investment in front line services such as housing 
maintenance, library operations, street cleaning and maintenance of open spaces, 
• Supporting economic development and the business communities,  through 
assistance and investment in facilities   
• Delivering funds to invest in infrastructure projects that will help sustain our 
communities across the County 
• Continuation of the progressive investment in area services with a focus on our 
towns & villages across the County 
• Supporting the development of the County aligned to the overall financial 
sustainability.   
The Draft Budget as presented attempts to strike the appropriate balance between the 
multiplicity of priorities and service demands.  
The overall budget strategy is an iterative process based on specific building blocks to 
arrive at the presentation of the statutory Draft Budget for adoption by Members. 
Throughout this process, the Council’s Corporate Policy Group (CPG) played a critical role 
in preparing this Budget. The CPG has been regularly consulted at a series of meetings 
since June 2025, with meetings in June, July, September, October, and November on the 
key objectives for the 2026 Budget.  The key stages for 2026 Draft Budget include: 
 
• Decision by the Council in July on the adjustment factor to the Local Property Tax 
(LPT) to vary the basic rate of LPT upward by 15% (10% 2025). 
• Consultation with the Corporate Policy Group (CPG) with initial CPG meetings 
held on 3rd June, 1st July, 2nd September and further Meetings on the 7th October, 
21st October and 4th November.

v 
 
• Briefing to Council at Development Committee meeting on the 7th November. 
• Consideration of Municipal District Draft Budgetary Plans, including the General 
Municipal Allocations, for 2026 at their budgetary meetings in October 2025. 
 
In preparing the draft budget the main priority has been to maintain, and where funding 
allowed, increase  the level of service provision across our key areas. Primary features in 
the preparation of Draft Budget 2026 include: 
• Maintaining and enhancing existing service levels  
• Focus on housing provision and our commitment to the delivery of Housing for All 
programme across the county 
• Increasing focus into our operations in the key towns and villages 
• Supporting economic development  
• Investment in operational resources  
• Providing for statutory requirements 
• Delivery of projects in a sustainable way and meeting climate action targets 
• Internal own resource funding to meet our infrastructure project needs and match 
funding requirements, as identified in the Council’s Capital Programme. The 
Capital Programme will continue to be assessed over 2026 to determine which 
schemes will advance over the coming years. 
 
 
Inflation & Economic Context 
 
Over recent years, our economy has experienced significantly high levels of inflation with 
higher consumer prices and business costs not only affect households and business, but 
also the Council’s spending capacity. This presents a key challenge and is placing 
increased pressure on all our services including housing maintenance, street-cleaning, 
and roads maintenance. 
 
Rising Demands & Costs 
The current consumer price index as of September 2025 is 2.7%, meaning that €1000 
worth of goods/services in 2024 now cost €1,027. To frame this for Budget 2026, an 
additional €8.5m is required in Budget 2026 simply to maintain services at 2025 levels.  
 
Putting this in the context of operational budgets and frontline services, additional 
expenditure has been required in Civic Amenity Sites between 2022 and 2025, 
representing a 9% increase as a result of inflationary pressures. Similarly, more than a 
30% increase has been allocated to the street cleaning budgets between 2022 and 2025 
which is a €1m increase in that timeframe. 
 
In addition, unmetered electricity is under a new contract spanning November 2024 to 
October 2027 which will see a 28.7% increase over the span of the contract as a result of

vi 
 
delayed impacts from the energy spikes in 2022. A new fixed contract for metered 
electricity is expected for January 2026 to December 2028 – it is expected that costs will 
remain largely similar in this regard, while our current contract for gas expires in 
September 2027. 
 
This presents a key challenge with pressure placed on provision of all our services and 
the need to find efficiencies to maintain delivery levels. The Draft budget presented takes 
account of Members views and  concerns, the need for additional resource to allow for 
the increase in service demands, e.g. increase in housing stock and library amenities, and 
in parallel trying to cover increased inflation construction and energy costs. 
 
 
Income Sources 2026 
 
 
 
 
 
Local Property Tax Allocation 2026 
 
The LPT approach for 2026 differed from 2025 with a revaluation of LPT taking place, 
following the Finance (Local Property Tax and Other Provisions) (Amendment) Act 2025. 
This led to changes in both the overall LPT yield and the yield in each local authority area.  
The LPT allocation model for 2026 is: 
• 100% of the estimated yield will be retained locally within the local authority area  
• 100% local retention of LPT means a surplus for those authorities with LPT income 
above their baseline, this applies to Cork County:  
o such authorities now retain a proportion of that surplus for their own use, 
equivalent to a maximum of 31% of the pre-variation yield (22.5% 2025).  
o Any local authority who benefits from the move to 31% retention are expected 
to use this additional funding for urban regeneration programmes in their 
areas. For Cork County the Department has advised that €3.2m of additional 
LPT is allocated to Urban Regeneration.

As outlined not all of this is available to use at the Council’s discretion, with the

Cork County Council with an increase of €3.4m compared to 2025.  
 
In July 2025, Cork County Council decided to vary the basic rate of LPT upwards by 15%

The decision of Council to vary the basic rate of LPT by 15% (10% 2025) generated an 
additional €1.9m for the Council. In recognition of a number of capital priorities at MD 
level, this additional funding of €1.9m per annum over the four-year period of 2026 to 
2029 is ringfenced for the Municipal Districts. This represents a direct fund of €7.6m 
aligned to the commitment of an LAF of 15% over the period 2026 to 2029, and will lead 
to a significant injection of resources into Municipal Districts to deliver long established 
critical local priorities. Such priorities would be delivered within the 4-year term aligned 
with the increased LAF of 15%.  
 
 
Grant Income 
The budget has been finalised on the basis that grant allocations received for 2025 will 
continue into 2026. Where adjustments have been made, increases, or decreases, it is 
grounded on discussions with the relevant National Government Departments. It should 
be noted that final grant allocations will not be known until 2026 and where grants are 
increased/ decreased this will be reflected in the delivery of services on the ground. 
 
 
Commercial Rates  
 
Cork County Council is a multi-faceted authority which has always focused on creating 
the best possible environment for the business community and citizens of Cork County.

viii 
 
Over the years, the Council has continued to enhance our economic development 
measures to support and nurture our commercial sector, to make Cork a better place in 
which to work and live.  
 
Commercial Rates is a significant contributor to the total budgeted income for the Council 
accounting for 27% of overall income. Cork County Council continues to work closely 
with Tailte Éireann to ensure that income potential is maximised through timely 
valuations, and with its rates payers to ensure collection rates remain high while 
supporting business sustainability. 
 
As highlighted in the table below increases in our commercial rates have not kept pace 
with inflation over the last 10 years, with a shortfall on ARV v CPI of 15.6%. This has led 
to a reduction in spending power and budget capacity to provide services. If the ARV had 
tracked with the CPI over the last decade, this would have resulted in approximately an 
additional €20million in rates income which would have been available to Cork County 
Council for the provision of services.

The Council is presenting this budget with an increase of 3% in the Annual Rate on 
Valuation (ARV) for commercial rates. In preparing the Draft Budget an extensive work 
program reviewed delivery programmes and budgets within each Division to exploit 
efficiencies and maximise income sources where possible and prudent. However, in order 
to prepare a balanced budget an increase in the ARV for Commercial Rates was still 
required. 
The Council recognises the difficulties faced by Rates Customers across the County. 
However, to maintain and enhance service delivery, and to facilitate the provision of 
several strategic initiatives in 2026 this increase is necessary. The increase in ARV of 3% 
generates an additional €4.2m of income for Cork County Council. This income will help  
fund the provision of key strategic initiatives and enhanced frontline services such as: 
• Investment in services to focus on towns and villages and upkeep works in each 
Municipal District 
• Provision for the acquisition of economic development land to support businesses 
and start-ups,  
• Annual rolling fund to support a programme for the taking in charge of estates 
• Provisions to support ongoing and future capital projects across the county

ix

National Revaluation Programme 
On 23 July 2025, Tailte Éireann published signed Valuation Orders for the rating 
authority areas of Cork County and Cork City Councils. The signing of the Valuation 
Orders follows the completion of a statutory consultation process between Tailte 
Éireann, the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage, and the Local 
Authorities involved.

x 
 
The revaluation is part of a national programme to modernise the rateable valuation of 
all commercial and industrial property in the State. The purpose of the revaluation is to 
bring increased transparency and more equity to the local authority rating system. 
Following revaluation, there is a much closer and uniform relationship between the 
current annual rental values of rateable properties and their commercial rates liability.   
Tailte Éireann issued correspondence to Ratepayers in July as the first step in the process 
with ratepayers. The new valuations for the areas undergoing revaluation will be 
published in 2027 and become effective for rates purposes from 2028 onwards. 
 
Local Government Rates and Other Matters Act 2019 (as amended) - Rates waiver 
scheme (section 15), and a rates vacancy abatement scheme (section 9) 
 
The Local Government Rates and Other Matters Act 2019 (as amended) provided for new 
rates waiver (section 15) scheme, and a rates vacancy abatement scheme (section 9), to 
be decided by local authority members in order to promote national and/or local policy 
objectives. A report on both schemes will accompany the Chief Executives Report and 
Draft Budget. The approval of these schemes is a reserved function of the elected 
members and are provided and accounted for within Draft Budget 2026. 
 
S15 RATES WAIVER SCHEME 2026  
The S15 Rates Waiver proposal was discussed with and endorsed by the Economic 
Development SPC and formed part of the budget discussions with CPG. The scheme is 
provided for in the Draft Budget 2026. The proposed rates waiver scheme supports 
objectives outlined in Cork County Council’s County Development Plans (CDP), Local 
Economic and Community Plans (LECP) and also the National Planning Framework 
(NPF). 
• Rates Waiver Scheme part (a) 
Cork County Council operates a Rates Incentive Scheme with a primary focus to 
assist Small and Medium Enterprises (SME’s), who comprise the majority of 
Ratepayers.  The scheme provides support to smaller enterprises in our towns and 
villages. This support aids the continuation of businesses across the County, 
maintaining local employment, sustaining the local economy and helping 
community, social and economic development.  
This scheme will now form part of the 2026 s15 rates waiver and will apply with 
existing timeframe on the following basis:  
- 
Scheme to apply to all ratepayers countywide.

xi 
 
- 
Relief at 3.5% of annual bill, capped at maximum bill of €7,000; i.e. the max 
relief any ratepayer will receive is 3.5% of €7,000 = €245  
 
• Rates Waiver Scheme part (b) 
This element of the rates waiver scheme aims to to support Vacancy, Dereliction 
and Town Centre First priorities. The rates waiver will incentivise the use of 
derelict and long-term vacant property, in specified locations. By encouraging the 
occupation of long-term vacant premises, the Council will support the 
improvement in appearance and attraction of the commercial properties and 
thereby will contribute indirectly to increased footfall for existing businesses. 
Aims of the Scheme 
• To encourage and support a qualifying business that might occupy vacant 
commercial or industrial premises  
• To facilitate opportunities for new businesses which have been established  
• To facilitate the development of new retail, office and related commercial and 
industrial services that will revitalise commercial centres in the County. 
• To support new business creation as a means of generating new vibrancy in 
Towns and villages within the County. 
• To demonstrate the serious commitment of the Council to contribute to 
economic development and regeneration across the County. 
 
For the first year of this waiver the scheme is targeted to certain towns. Based on 
consultation with our Property Activation Unit, in light of vacancy surveys and 
Town Centre First priorities , Kanturk, Mallow and Youghal would be highlighted 
for consideration.  An application may be deemed ineligible if it has the potential 
to lead to displacement of existing enterprises. The rates waiver will apply on a 
sliding basis over 3 years. 
• End of Year 1 Rates waiver of 75% of rate levied for subject year (i.e. 12 
month period of trading starting at date of occupancy). 
• End of Year 2 Rates waiver of  50% of rate levied for subject year. 
• End of Year 3 Rates waiver of 25% of rate levied for subject year. 
 
The Scheme is applicable to the use of existing rated commercial properties that 
have been listed as vacant for a minimum of 2 years (31st December each year).   
 
Competition Clause: 
Potential displacement will be a primary concern in determining the eligibility of 
any application to the scheme.  The executive may deem a project to be ineligible if 
it has the potential to lead to displacement of existing enterprises.

xii 
 
Eligibility 
The Scheme will be available to: 
• a newly established business 
• an existing business relocating or expanding from outside the County 
• an existing business maintaining current location and expanding into a new 
location. 
 
 
S9 RATES VACANCY ABATEMENT SCHEME 2026 
The Local Government Rates and Other Matters Act 2019 (as amended) section 9 
provides for the abatement of rates in respect of vacant property: 
• Provides that a local authority may provide a temporary abatement of rates for 
vacant properties. 
• Allows for greater flexibility and customisation of schemes than before, allowing 
them to be made for class or classes of liable persons or properties, and to be used 
as a tool to discourage commercial vacancy. 
• Offers Councils the scope to introduce rates abatement on vacant property 
schemes for a wide variety of purposes. 
 
Vacancy abatement for 2026 
As for 2025, it is recommended that the level of Vacancy Abatement Rate be renewed, 
without amendment, at 100% for 2026: 
• No submissions have been received following  the public consultation process  
• as it is being maintained at 100% it will have no financial effect on the Council’s 
Budget for 2026.  
• The Rates Waiver Scheme provides incentive for the use of vacant premises. 
 
Following from the Budget consultation and engagement with CPG we are committed to 
engage early with Members to review the potential for customisation of the current 
vacancy abatement scheme for 2027. This will be done early in 2026  in preparation for 
Budget 2027. This will allow full consideration of options and implications and allow the 
development of a robust scheme to support utilisation of vacant property.

xiii 
 
Budget 2026 Strategic Benefits 
 
 Economic Development 
The Council continues to be proactive in driving economic development across the 
County and is very conscious of the need to support our business sector and to 
underpin the sustainability of our communities. To that end, Draft 2026 Budget 
continues to provide for: 
• Economic Development Fund supporting tourism and strategic marketing 
initiatives, partnerships with local and regional stakeholders, and the co-funding 
for economic development initiatives.  
• Dedicated Property Activation and Regeneration Unit (PARU), supported by the 
EDF and continues to proactively engage with internal and external stakeholders 
to examine and action opportunities for property activation and town centre 
regeneration.  
• Town Centre Regeneration Fund recognising the levels of vacancy and dereliction 
in towns and villages and the need to innovate to solve these problems.  
• Economic Development land acquisition with an increased budget of €0.5m 
included to build the funding reserve for the expansion of our land bank. This is 
one of the measures being financed by the 3% Rates increase income. 
• The Town Development Fund (TDF) and Village Enhancement Fund (VEF) are 
recognised as being of significant value to the Municipal Districts. It is critically 
important that the core principle of supporting town & village development, in 
particular the vitality of the retail, hospitality, and services sector core of our 
towns, is the primary criteria for the spending on this fund. It is intended to engage 
with the MD Members to consider the alignment of the TDF €0.95m and VEF 
€0.55m to co-fund strategic projects early in 2026. 
• Our Local Enterprise Offices (LEO) continue to engage with the business 
community and provide support both financially and through mentoring and 
training. The LEOs serve as a first stop shop to providing support and services to 
start, grow and develop micro businesses in the County.  
However, it must be noted the Council’s investment in the economic development of the 
County is not solely confined to direct investment and supports for enterprises. €3.2m of 
the 2026 LPT allocation is ringfenced to self-fund Urban Regeneration work which will 
support town and village development and sustain local economies. The Council invests 
own resources across its services to make the region an attractive proposition for 
economic growth, to benefit communities and fortify our rates base. This investment 
includes maintenance and development of the transportation network, providing 
recreation and amenity facilities, developing communities both rural and in towns, and 
investing in the culture and heritage of the area. Through this the Council provides  
improved quality of life for potential workers, new remote workers, and new citizens.

xiv 
 
Our County Development Plan adopted in 2022 outlines the opportunities and the 
strategy for sustainable development across the County and lays the foundations for 
continued economic development. This is reflected in the ambitious Capital Programme 
2026-28 and highlights the need for our Annual Budget to provide the necessary funding 
to deliver these projects. 
 
 Towns & Villages 
The Draft budget 2026 continues the Council’s commitment to municipal area services 
and resourcing including: 
• Retention of Town Presentation Teams in each MD (key towns and villages) 
• Preparation of Town Enhancement Plan for 2026 
• Expansion of Community Wardens from 4 to 9, 1 for each area district.  
The Community Wardens will focus on road openings inspection, hedge cutting notices, 
casual trading and outdoor street furniture compliance, litter management, Beach bye 
laws and inspection of parks and open spaces among others. 
 
 Taking in Charge of Estates 
The Draft Budget contains an increased provision of €0.5m (€0.2m 2025), which is an 
ongoing annual provision towards the funding gap and progression of the taking in 
charge of estates across the County. This one of the measures being financed by the 3% 
Rates increase income. 
 
 Capital Programme Own Resources Funding 
The Council’s Draft Budget reflects the Council’s continued commitment to aid the 
development and support of our communities, our towns, villages and supporting 
hinterland. The Capital Programme encompasses the current and potential 
infrastructural projects to be undertaken for the years 2026 - 2028. It outlines a proposed 
investment of over €1.3bn across the entire range of activities including housing, library 
provision, recreation and amenity, economic development & tourism, transportation and 
active travel measures, public realm, coastal protection, and flood relief. At least 15% of 
this programme required Council own local funding to match available grants, and for 
infrastructure projects that are fully funded by our own resources.  
The Draft Budget includes a provision towards financing this local funding whether 
through bank financing or internal loans, with a Capital Projects fund of €3m part 
financed by the increase in commercial rates. This increases our internal loans budget to 
provide resources  towards the Council’s’ match funding requirements for RRDF and 
URDF which will be required  for projects such as Midleton Town Centre improvement, 
Fermoy, Mallow, Cobh, and Skibbereen Public Realm improvements.

xv 
 
Examples of infrastructure projects requiring own resources include playgrounds, car 
parking, public lighting, and public toilets. In addition, Cork County Council need to have 
internal own resources to match fund the development of libraries, to fund upgrade of 
our swimming pools, and invest in our marine infrastructure. The three year Capital 
Programme identifies over €200m of own resource funding to progress the delivery of a 
number of these projects, and the programme of projects will need to be prioritised based 
on the funding available. This internal funding need requires a critical assessment of the 
capital programme to evaluate which schemes will advance over the coming years.  
 
Sustainability and Climate  
Sustainability is a key objective of Cork County Council and integral to all our activities. 
The Council’s investment in Climate Action is not solely confined to direct investment and 
supports. We are committed to continuing to mainstream Climate Action in the delivery 
of our services and affecting change in terms of climate adaptation through initiatives 
and actions to adapt our practices including:  
• Public Lighting Energy Efficiency Project (PLEEP)  
• Fleet Management Unit energy management and fuel alternatives 
• Sustainable Transport & Active Travel Programme 
• Energy retrofitting & efficiencies and LED lighting in 200 Council properties 
• Housing Energy Efficiency Retrofitting Programme (EERP), aided by DHLGH,  
• Flood Management and Protection Schemes  
• Biodiversity & Ecosystem Protection  
• Public Awareness & Community engagement. 
Members will be aware that national Climate Action legislation commits Ireland to net-
zero emissions by 2050 and a 51% reduction by 2030. Recent severe weather events 
around the globe and locally confirm that Climate Change is real. The Local Authority 
Climate Action Plan (LACAP) is facilitating the development of annual implementation 
programmes that will have regard to the targets the Council is required to meet, and the 
budgets available from local and national government sources and from private sector 
sources where available.   
 
 
Draft Budget 2026 – Service Areas 
 
The Draft Annual Budget is €530m in 2026, an increase on 2025 (€516m).  
 
In framing this Budget, Cork County Council has been conscious of the inflationary 
pressures that are currently facing operations. Balancing the budget has required a 
balancing of priorities. When considering the financial resources available the Council

xvi 
 
has had to reconfigure the budget and delivery methods, finding efficiencies and, where 
required allocate additional funding to ensure there is no impact on service delivery. 
The Draft Budget 2026 has not been able to meet the totality of service expectations of 
the Directorates. The increased expenditure demands are not being matched by sufficient 
income buoyancy thereby limiting our ability to meet the level of expectation for services. 
However, throughout the budget preparation process the executive has worked to review 
financial resources and configure these to ensure the continuation of service delivery.  
 
The Draft Budget 2026 continues provision for key areas including: 
 
Housing 
• In response to increasing demands on service and increasing costs due to 
inflationary pressures the draft budget provides for an increase of €2.9m for our 
housing stock across: 
o Day to Day repairs 1m 
o Voids and Energy Efficiency Programme 1m 
o Planned Maintenance Programme 0.5m 
o Heat Pump Upgrades 0.4m 
• Continuation of our VOIDs programme of over €6.4m  
• Croí Cónaithe Towns Grant is among the suite of measures under the pathway to 
addressing vacancy and efficient use of existing stock in Housing for All. There is 
a provision of €13.2m included for the delivery of this program, a decrease of 
€4.8m, reflecting an over provision for Budget 2025; this is shown on both income 
and expenditure. 
• Homeless Emergency Accommodation budget of €7.8m which is a reduction on 
2025 and reflects the reduction in the activity in these services. 
• €8.9m has been included for Housing Grants for Housing Aid Older People, 
Housing Adaption Grant & Housing Mobility Grant an increase of €0.6m.                                              
• €19.5m is provided for the delivery of the Payment and Availability Scheme, an 
increase of €3.6m on 2025. This expenditure is matched by Income as this 
expenditure is 100% recoupable.  
• Social Housing PPP Programme Bundle 2 and Bundle 6. This is a partnership 
between the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH), 
the Local Authorities involved, the National Development Finance Agency (NDFA) 
and a specially formed Project Company (PPP Co.). Budget 2026 includes income 
and corresponding expenditure of €10m for the delivery of Bundle 2, a small 
reduction on 2025.  
• The above increases are being aided by the increase in Cork County Councils 
housing stock, the annual rolling rent review and the additional Cost Rental units 
which together will generate an additional buoyancy in Housing Rents of 
approximately €4.5m.

xvii 
 
 
Roads and Transportation 
• The Roads Budget for 2026 has been increased to reflect the increasing cost of 
fuel, electricity, and materials.  
• Grant allocations for national local and regional roads are in line with expectations 
for 2026 based on engagement with TII and are subject to change. There is a 
reduction on both income and expenditure reflecting the additional storm related 
allocations received in 2025. The allocations for the year will not be known until 
early 2026 and budgets will be adjusted to account for these when announced. 
• Public lighting provision has been increased to €0.4m and an additional €50,000 for 
asset replacement. Also, the funding for the loan repayment of the public lighting 
energy efficiency project is reflected in Div B for 2026. 
• Pay Parking Dividend – provision is made for the continuation of a dividend of 
€270,000 in 2026 which is dependent on realisation of the parking income.  
• Funding of €0.6m for Speed Limit Signs matched by income 
• In addition, the following strategic and operational additional budgets are 
included which are aided by the increase in the ARV for rates 
 Retention of the strategic provision for Roads Relief Design Works €0.25m 
 Provision for Contribution to Footpath Programme €0.5m 
 Provision for Traffic Safety Measures €0.18m 
 Roads Own Resources Funding €1.1m.

Housing Rent Collection 
The Rent Collection Unit has county wide responsibility for the management and collection of rents from 
social housing tenants and RAS tenants.  The unit also has responsibility for initiating legal action where 
rent payments are not made.  The importance of early prevention of rent arrears is accepted as the most 
effective way to protect the Council’s income and prevent low-income tenants accruing debts which can 
be very difficult to clear.  
 
The rent charged by Cork County Council is based on a differential rent scheme where the rent is 
calculated based on the assessable income of the principal earner together with a contribution from any 
subsidiary earner in the household. The minimum weekly rent is €25 and there is no maximum rent. The 
Rent Collection Unit manages rent appeals under the Rent Appeal Policy and if the Council feels that the 
amount of a rent calculated under the Differential Rent Scheme would give rise to hardship in a 
household, it may agree to accept a lesser weekly rent for a specified time.  
 
The Rent Assessment Unit is responsible for carrying out rent assessments. A full rent review of tenants’ 
rents is currently underway and will continue in 2026. This ensures that rents are based on current 
household incomes and updated occupancy details. It is expected that all housing rental income in 2026 
will be €32m.

Affordable Housing: 
The Affordable Housing Scheme is designed to help people bridge the gap between what a person can 
afford to pay and the price of a new home. 
 
Cork County Council is making newly built homes available at a reduced price for first-time and other

affordability is an issue. 
 
The Council takes a percentage equity share in the home equal to the difference between the open 
market value of the home and the reduced price paid.  This means that if a person buys a home at a 20% 
reduction on the open market value, the local authority will have a 20% equity share in the home. 
To date, the Council has launched a total of 245 affordable homes in Mallow, Carrigaline, Cobh, Fermoy, 
Bandon, Midleton, Bantry, Macroom, Carrigtwohill and Youghal with further schemes due to be advertised

Active Land Management 
Active Land Management by Planning Authorities is described by Government as follows: 
‘Preparation of development plans is only an initial step. Plan implementation is key … to enable planning 
authorities to more dynamically lead and manage the development process in their areas, ensuring that 
land zoned for development comes into use as anticipated in development plans and in tandem with 
supporting infrastructure.’ (Planning Policy Statement 2015) 
 
The Council’s Active Land Management (ALM) activities are divided into two work programmes, as 
follows: 
1. Statutory Land Activation Processes. 
2. Development Lands Monitoring and Reporting.  
 
 
1. Statutory Land Activation Processes: - 
 
Vacant Sites Register & Levy: 
The Vacant Site Levy (VSL) is a housing land activation tool and its function is to promote development 
rather than as a revenue generating mechanism. The Vacant Sites Register & Levy applies to certain 
Residentially Zoned Sites and Regeneration Areas identified in statutory Development Plans. The 
Council’s Register was established in 2016 and has a direct impact on sites on the Register (via the 
imposition of a Levy at 7% of the market value of the land), as well as an in-direct impact on additional 
‘candidate’ sites – where it is observed that the VSL impacts on landowner considerations.    
 
The administration of the Vacant Sites Register / Levy has regard to the dynamic nature of the process 
as set out in the Urban Regeneration and Housing Act 2015 (as amended), with the status of lands liable 
to change during implementation of the Levy process. The Council’s Vacant Sites Register is: 
 One of the most active Register nationally since 2016, with more than 40 no. housing 
development sites being processed through its Register. The Register currently has three 
remaining sites listed. 
 As of 2022 for which collated national figures are available, CCC is one of 13 LAs to have 
collected Levies; and, 
 All Levies issued remain as a charge on the land. Levy payments to date appear to be linked to 
development activation or when land ownership changes.

Residential Zoned Land Tax: 
Government introduced the Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT) under the Finance Act 2021, intended 
to replace the Vacant Site Levy. Following the introduction of the Residential Zoned Land Tax, a 
comprehensive review of all residential delivery lands in the County’s 32 main settlements that meet the 
requirements of the Government’s RZLT initiative was undertaken by Cork County Council to inform the 
mapping required under the process. 
 
The criteria for the identification of residential delivery lands were broadened under the RZLT process 
from that of the Vacant Site Levy process, widening the scope of the potential residential lands that may 
be included. Agricultural lands are included for consideration under the RZLT process.  
 
The RZLT is an annual statutory process that requires Local Authorities to publish a Final Annual Map 
on January 31st annually. Currently almost 400 no. residential delivery sites are identified by Cork County 
Council in the Council’s Annual RZLT Map, ranging in scale from small infill housing development sites 
to larger scheme housing delivery sites. The number of sites identified by Cork County Council’s RZLT 
mapping is one of the largest nationally.  
 
Any RZLT liability arising from this process is managed by Revenue and the deadline for tax returns 
under the RZLT by Landowners is May 25th annually.  
 
During the 2025 RZLT process landowners of lands that are in use for a bona fide economic use 
(including agriculture use) and are not the subject of extant planning permission for housing development 
were facilitated in requesting a change of zoning that would remove them from future RZLT mapping (and 
from future tax liability). Cork County Council received 12 no. requests for change of zoning during 2025 
and a change of zoning process (CDP Variation) for 11 no. sites is underway (the additional site is under 
active housing construction and therefore does not meet the required criteria). It is proposed that the 
Variation process will be completed in Q1 2026.

EU Green Deal. Not delivering on the EU Green Deal requirements will potentially result in significant

Offshore Wind Industrial Strategy, which sets out a target of 5GW of installed ORE by 2030 and 37GW

Through the development of domestic renewable energy capacities, as well as energy storage and 
transmission technologies and infrastructure, Ireland will move away from its reliance on imported fossil 
fuels. This will deliver multiple strategic benefits to the State, including sustainable environmental 
stewardship, climate change mitigation, energy independence, security of energy supply and economic 
development opportunities.

offering innovative value propositions to the offshore wind sector both at home and overseas. 
 Ireland to become a high potential market for foreign direct investment (FDI) to complement our 
domestic capability. 
 Maximise the economic benefit of achieving Ireland and Europe’s ORE targets by creating a solid 
domestic supply chain and resilient ORE industry. 
 Maximise the economic impact of future renewable energy use, leveraging the full potential of 
additional generation capacity that will arise from achieving our ORE targets.
